# **User Manual Instructions**

Supplement to the book *[Never Search Alone](https://www.amazon.com/Never-Search-Alone-Seekers-Playbook/dp/B0B9Q9YDQ5)*  
By Phyl Terry  
All Rights Reserved

**Overview**  
This toolkit is part of the broader set of exercises and tools in *Never Search Alone*.

This one is designed to help leaders and their teams work better together through learning each other’s ‘user manual.’

Adam Medros, the President of edX, a consortium of universities started by Harvard and MIT, creates what he calls blueprints as a tool to help his teams work better together and with him.  
   
The concept is simple, and he learned it from his-then colleague at TripAdvisor, Luc Levesque.   
   
The purpose is to write down key aspects of how you work including any weaknesses or foibles you may have. You share this blueprint, user manual, or readme file (the same kind of document goes by three different names) with your team as a way to ask them to help you be a better leader *and* to help them learn how to work with you.  
   
For example, Adam tells his teams through his blueprint that he’s someone who can react too quickly and that if that were to happen on an important topic they should persevere and trust that he will eventually slow down to hear them out. He may not end up agreeing with their proposed course of action, but, if they ask him to go slower, he will pull back from being dismissive.   
   
This is not an uncommon challenge for leaders with many competing priorities. A blueprint is a good way to forewarn your teams to help you be the better leader you want to be and not a Doonesbury caricature.  
   
It’s also a great way to onboard new team members. In fact, that was the original reason that Luc Levesque created a blueprint approach back in 2013\.

# User Manuals for Leaders (and their teams) {#user-manuals-for-leaders-(and-their-teams)}

By Hope Gurion and Phil Terry

Adam Medros, the President of edX, a consortium of universities started by Harvard and MIT, creates what he calls blueprints as a tool to help his teams work better together and with him.  
   
The concept is simple, and he learned it from his-then colleague at TripAdvisor, Luc Levesque.   
   
The purpose is to write down key aspects of how you work including any weaknesses or foibles you may have. You share this blueprint, user manual, or readme file (the same kind of document goes by three different names) with your team as a way to ask them to help you be a better leader *and* to help them learn how to work with you.  
   
For example, Adam tells his teams through his blueprint that he’s someone who can react too quickly and that if that were to happen on an important topic they should persevere and trust that he will eventually slow down to hear them out. He may not end up agreeing with their proposed course of action, but, if they ask him to go slower, he will pull back from being dismissive.   
   
This is not an uncommon challenge for leaders with many competing priorities. A blueprint is a good way to forewarn your teams to help you be the better leader you want to be and not a Doonesbury caricature.  
   
It’s also a great way to onboard new team members. In fact, that was the original reason that Luc Levesque created a blueprint approach back in 2013, as he told the New York Times and then later me in a subsequent interview.   
   
His coach originally helped him create the idea when he was growing the team at his startup, TravelPod, which he later sold to TripAdvisor.   
   
I was hiring about five new people, and I remember talking to my executive coach about it and thinking: “Now I have to go through that whole process again. This is going to take forever.” And that’s when I went back and forth with my coach, and we thought, “Wouldn’t it be great if you had a blueprint to give someone on Day 1 that encapsulates what works for me and what are some of the quirks about me…” So, I wrote it up, and started sharing it with my team. It’s worked really well.  
   
Colleen Hancock, Council moderator and longtime COO at BabyCenter, uses another approach that she has borrowed from her personal therapy.  
   
All of my teams definitely know my foibles and I give them a safe word to tell me. I learned this through marriage counseling – that I had to give my husband a safe word to use with me because sometimes I can run a mile a minute. I’m going fast because I've got so many things on my plate but that's not fair to him, or, when I’m at work, to the person trying to talk with me. So, I tell them to use the safe word and I will honor it and slow down.   
   
David Krauter, a longtime Council member, believes that a big part of his job is to really understand how his teams are working together and how they perceive him (how he’s doing and what blind spots he might be having). Like many other Council leaders, he has applied methods from product management and customer experience to his leadership practice.  
   
I grew up in a product role, and in product you're kind of the hub of the wheel, so the way that I viewed my leadership philosophy as ‘I'm only as good as my team is, and how well I can work with my teams.’ So, the better I can understand how I'm perceived by the team on whether I'm doing well or not, then the better I can lead the team. As I moved into more executive management roles, this approach has stayed with me. As a result, I have used a number of approaches like blueprints, personality tests, 360 feedback.  
   
Jenna Hammer, the Senior Manager of User Research at Zillow, has a wiki she’s created for her growing team that reflects her management philosophy and how she likes to communicate and make decisions. This wiki helps her both ask her team for help and onboard new hires.  
   
For example, Hammer, unlike Medros, does not react quickly. In fact, she tells her team via her wiki that she needs time to “think through details, develop a point-of-view, and come back with a decision.”  
   
We recommend something like a blueprint, user manual, or read me file to all Council members because it helps clarify values, create an operating system, and is a great way to ask for help to be a better leader.   
   
In fact, we recommend not only that members do it for their teams, but that they also share their user manuals with their Councils so that members can better understand each other.

## Generating User Manuals {#generating-user-manuals}

See also:

- Luc Levesque’s [2013 interview in the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/02/business/luc-levesque-of-trip-advisor-on-frequent-evaluations.html)  
- FirstRound Capital’s [write-up on User Manuals](https://firstround.com/review/the-indispensable-document-for-the-modern-manager/)

### Step 1: 3-5 Lessons You’ve Learned {#step-1:-3-5-lessons-you’ve-learned}

One way to warm-up to start your user manual is to do an exercise on the 3-5 key lessons you’ve learned in your career. 

Adam Medros has done this with his leadership team at EdX and found it very helpful as a way to both build trust with his team and to help his team write their user manuals. 

He ran this exercise with this simple question:

What are 3-5 lessons you’ve learned (what was the experience where you learned the lesson) that have shaped a principle you believe in?

Medros said that this was “a good way to think about what’s important to me and to each of my colleagues and why.” He explained that, for example, the question helped him explore why he believes in Transparency as a key principle and thus think back to the experience that first made him see the value of it. 

### Step 2: Write your own User Manual {#step-2:-write-your-own-user-manual}

Imagine how much easier work would be if everyone had a user manual \- clear instructions on how best to work with each other. The goal of this exercise is to develop our individual user manuals so we can learn better how to work together successfully. 

Think about how you work. When have you been super happy in a team or context? What values of yours were honored by the team in that context? When have you been unhappy? What values of yours were not being honored in that context? What do these reflections tell you about what it is that makes you tick and feel motivated and supported at work? 

Some prompting questions:

**Management Style Prompts**

* I would describe my management style as ...  
* I value …   
* I appreciate ..  
* I don’t have patience for …   
* Here’s what I expect from my team  
* Here’s how I think about 1on1s …   
* Things I need from my team are …   
* How you can help me is … 

**Feedback Prompts**

* I prefer getting feedback in this way….  
* I am most comfortable giving feedback this way….  
* I don’t react well to….

**Communication Prompts**

* My preferred channels of communication are….  
* My expectations around communication responses are ...  
* I like asynchronous processing \- send me pre-reads for meaty topics / I prefer to process information synchronously during the meeting (don’t send me long pre-reads)   
* The best way to communicate with me is … 

**Workstyle Prompts**

* My work habits include …   
* Here’s how I work with my team…  
* Conditions I like to work in are …   
* Activities that give me energy are …  
* Activities that deplete me are …  
* My pet peeves are …  
* Things that don’t allow me to be at my best are ...  
* Things I need from my (coworkers, managers, environment etc.)   
* My preferred working hours are….  
* I am a morning person so … / I am a night owl so …  
* People who have worked with me a long time have realized that….  
* My decisions and actions are driven by … 

**Motivation Prompts**

* I learn best when …  
* When this happens, I react badly….  
* When this happens, I can do my best work….  
* I get excited about doing X….  
* I really avoid or procrastinate doing Y….  
* I thrive when…

   
**Capability Prompts**

* My unique abilities are …  
* Things I struggle with are …   
* Things I excel at are …   
* I am most comfortable / confident when … 

**Personal Prompts**

* My Myers Briggs type / colors test type // other thing that tells you about how I work is….  
* Something you may not know about me is….  
* Here’s what’s not flexible in my work/life….  
* What people misunderstand about me …   
* Some of my quirks are …   
* You can help me by …

# 1\. Woman Engineering Manager’s READMe {#1.-woman-engineering-manager’s-readme}

## Overview			 {#overview}

			  
●  In general I really crave feedback and am very responsive to constructive feedback. 	  
●  I am okay with feedback being delivered in person or writing or via \[Manager\].  
●  If feedback is delivered in person I prefer that it’s not delivered in a group setting and instead delivered in a 1:1 scenario.  
●  I like for feedback to be delivered to me intentionally over dynamically. Real time  
feedback can often be unedited and is not as well constructed as feedback that is thought out. This gives me a slight preference for written feedback over in person feedback. 			●  I always have feedback to give. I will always give feedback on what I think and how I feel about what is happening. Please feel free to tell me how or if you’d like feedback from me.  
 							

## My Name vs. My Pronouns {#my-name-vs.-my-pronouns}

There are significantly less women in engineering than there are men. It’s much more confusing to refer to individual men as he/him so they’re usually referred to by their names when discussed or referenced in conversation as they should be. Unfortunately I’ve begun to observe that I am referred to as she/her much more often than “\[NAME}” and it’s begun to bug me a lot. So, if you can manage to **use my name first and often** I’d much prefer it\!

## Tears		 {#tears}

		  
●  Crying is a biological response that I have to any strong emotion. 		  
●  Often when I’m crying I’m not feeling sad, but frustrated, angry, confused, annoyed, etc.  
●  I have very little control over when I cry or what will make me cry.				●  It is very likely that in working with me long enough you will experience my tears at some  point.  
●  **Do:** try to ignore that I’m crying and proceed as normal if possible. I’ll remove myself  
 from the room/conversation if I’m crying \*that\* much.  
●  **Don’t:** please don’t try to hug me or comfort me with any form of physical contact. It feels strange that I wouldn’t hug my coworkers normally and I don’t want a hug just because I started crying.  
 						

## Humor {#humor}

● Dealing in jokes and sarcasm is a preferred means of connection between me and peers. I’m very open to all feedback on my sense of humor/jokes and willing to recognize and apologize when I tell bad ones (I just want us all to have a laugh together sometimes).

## Gender {#gender}

●  I’m a woman in engineering at ..., and there aren’t a lot of those. I talk about this a lot.  
●  I went to a women’s college due to the biases I experienced with my male peers in high school. I’m very sensitive to gender dynamics and what it means to be one of the \~eight women in engineering at ....  
●  I don’t want to be treated differently because of my gender, and if it starts to happen I hope we can talk about it. Examples of ways someone might start to treat me differently include mansplaining, assuming I should always take notes, gender-related jokes, etc.  
 ●  Another thing that will likely happen is questions about how we can improve diversity at  
 .., what I want to do about it, or what I am doing about it. I’m mostly happy answering these questions, but I also want to know what your answers are.  
 ●  **Upshot**: being in a minority group and being different than nearly everyone else in a big way can be really hard. I want to be included and feel safe and happy. Thanks for reading this and helping me achieve that goal.

## Growth Areas					 					 {#growth-areas}

● Independently solving problems

○ I learn things better through dialogue over reading and searching for answers by myself; however, this can prevent me from building many of the skills necessary for solving a problem end to end alone. 

● Delivering feedback so that it may be effective.					

○ I always have thoughts and feedback to share, but could grow in my ability to enact positive change with critical feedback.

● Knowing when to speak my mind and when to hold my tongue

○ I am very assertive and opinionated and that is often a strength of mine but usually it’s a growth area. I am working on filtering my thoughts and assertive nature in a way that is actionable and solutions-oriented so that it’s helpful and not abrasive.

● Calibrating my emotions with my words in my communications.

○ I speak in a lot of hyperboles and am quick to show emotions and share my feelings amidst all of my thoughts. This can be confusing for people if I don’t explain how much something is upsetting me in context since it can look like I’m 10/10 \*VERY\* upset about something when I’m mildly annoyed sometimes since I’m not very good at hiding that I’m annoyed about something.

				

## Some Strengths {#some-strengths}

						 							  
●  Organizing people	  
●  Communicating my feelings and usually my thoughts.  
●  Thinking out loud  
 							  
Tech Background  
	  
●  Languages:

 ○  **Most comfortable:** Python, Java  
 ○  **Pretty comfortable:** Javascript, OCaml  
 ○  **Need more practice:** C, Scheme	

●  Frameworks:

○  Plone \- Python-based CMS platform similar to Django. One of my summer internships involved building a course creator CMS prototype for an ed-tech startup using Plone.  
○  Django \- some side projects/tutorials. Current work.  
○  Angular JS \- Google’s first version of Angular. It’s used in the front end of the tech stack for Google for Nonprofits  
 	  
●  Some projects:

○  Python scripting/analytics for MIT App Inventor.  
○  Virtual debugger features in JS for Pencil code  
○  Work in the python tech stack for NextThought.  
○  Work in Java/Angular tech stack with Google for Nonprofits.

## Things I Like {#things-i-like}

### In Work {#in-work}

●  Clear communication  
○  I appreciate when people ensure everyone’s on the same page before they dive in.  
 						  
○  To me communication is clear when no one is confused. How we achieve that may be situational.

●  Organization  
○ Having a clear structure or process for how a team is working makes it easier for me to operate. Sprints and agile process is a great example of organization that I gravitate towards.

● Fast decision making  
○ I tend to get annoyed with unnecessary back and forth in decision making where someone needs to take charge and I appreciate when someone advocates for a particular decision in order to move things forward.

●  Productivity

●  Problem solving  
					 							  
●  Collaboration  
	  
●  Post meeting surveys (really all surveys)

○ Anytime more than 3 people meet in a room, especially if they don’t meet fairly regularly, I like participating in post meeting surveys about that meeting. This practice is residual from my work at ... where surveys were everywhere, but I came to value the data in survey feedback and I really like the written medium and collective participation.

●  Calendars and schedules

* ○  I really like having a schedule and time clearly allocated throughout my day. That being said, I will gladly use my free time to chat with anyone who needs to grab me whenever and I am not bothered by being interrupted.  
*   
* ○  In general I prefer morning meetings over afternoon meetings. I am less focused post lunch and it’s harder to act on the meeting’s content within the time of the afternoon.  
*   
* ○  Scheduling same day meetings tends to bother me and I prefer for things to be planned ahead of time as often as possible; however, if you ping me to grab some time I am more than happy to work around calendars.  
* 

### In Life {#in-life}

●  Beer  
●  Poetry  
●  Art \- (modern. Not portraits)  
●  People (I spell extrovert as extravert because extrovert isn’t extra enough for me)

## Things I Hate {#things-i-hate}

### In Work {#in-work-1}

●  Lack of leadership/ownership/decision maker  
●  Feeling underutilized  
●  Engaging with and responding to combative or competitive attitudes. I’m not here to win anything. I’m here to work on a team and achieve together.  
●  Having the same conversation more than once. When I feel like I’m in a loop of rehashing something and not making progress I tend to get visibly frustrated and withdrawal.

### In Life {#in-life-1}

●  Mean people/jerks. If someone is mean to me I’ll take that as feedback that they want me to avoid them at all costs. (This makes teamwork very hard.)  
●  Exclusive organizations. **Inclusion is really important to me** and I will work extra hard to make sure everyone feels included around me.   
 						

					 				  
			  
		

# VP, GM, SVP {#vp,-gm,-svp}

## 1\. EVP of a Bank {#1.-evp-of-a-bank}

## Things I believe: {#things-i-believe:}

My job is to steward the vision, ask for outcomes, ensure alignment and clear the path

·   My first preoccupation is the strategy – but I’ll never do it alone.  Our vision should represent the best of our collective thinking.  
·   I should be asking you to deliver business outcomes versus dictating specific tactics.  Sometimes I need to dive in, but if you feel I’m in too deep, please feel free to tell me to back off (or back up\!).  
·   Great things happen when we truly get on the same page.  Let’s do the hard work to get there, and never pretend we are aligned if we aren’t.

### Intention {#intention}

Intent (really) matters.  Mistakes and misunderstandings happen.  I get it and believe that failing can be one of our best learning tools.  We all deserve a little grace.

### Bad News {#bad-news}

Bad news doesn’t age well.  Like everybody I love to hear good news.  But bring me the problems, the quandaries and the challenges right away.  I’d much rather help you solve them than hear about them after they’ve blown up. 

### Diversity {#diversity}

Diverse teams are the strongest teams.  Truly diverse teams include a full range of backgrounds.  We thrive when we have demographic diversity, diversity of thought, *and* an environment where that richness is cherished as being at the core of how we show up every day.

## Things I like: {#things-i-like:}

### Teams {#teams}

Being part of a team: I love being on a team and I love building a team.  I also love that companies are “teams of teams”. 

·   I deeply appreciate that \[company division\] has a track record of being ONE TEAM and that track record warmly includes everybody who touches our amazing customers  
·   I’m also committed to being part of the \[company name\]  team first. I think of a division as the offense or defense and the company as the overall (insert favorite sports) team.

### Good Debate {#good-debate}

Good debate leads to better decisions.  I really enjoy challenging ideas and having my ideas challenged.  I also don’t mind breaking ties when it’s time, because while it’s often preferable to emerge with a definitive answer, sometimes it’s best to “disagree and commit” so that we can move on to the next debate. 

### Feedback  {#feedback}

I want the good, the bad and the ugly – and I want to give you the same.  But I also want to give feedback that’s really meaningful.

·   I often take time to build up a pattern as I get to know people, because first impressions aren’t always right impressions.  Especially with people I may see less frequently, it may take a minute before I volunteer my opinion.  So…  
·   …ask anytime.  If you want to know what I think, PLEASE ask.  Even if I’m not yet sure…if you ask I’ll tell you what I know, what I think I know, and what I still don’t know.

## Things I want to do better: {#things-i-want-to-do-better:}

### I Can be Hard to Read {#i-can-be-hard-to-read}

I’m genuinely enthusiastic, but I can overdo it.  I like to say that I have a normal emotional range, but it tends to go from “fine” to “amazing” instead of the more typical “bad” to “good”.  I need to remember that not everything is “great” and sometimes I need to be asked “did you really think that thing was terrific?”

As a result, I can sometimes be hard to read. 

Both because I like to build up a pattern before I expound, and because I can be overly rosy, I get feedback that people don't always know what I *really think*.  Please ask me when that happens….I’ve got nothing to hide\!  Usually I’m just figuring it out myself. 

### Details {#details}

Sweat the small stuff.  I know, *they* say not to sweat the small stuff.  For me, sometimes I need to sweat the details more.  When I see an issue, I will go as deep as anyone can go, but I may not go deep enough if I don’t perceive a reason to dive.  Especially given that I’ll be in a new and unfamiliar context, I’ll need help knowing where I need to know what I don’t already know…

## How I work: {#how-i-work:}

### I want to know your cadence {#i-want-to-know-your-cadence}

I want everyone to be able to bring their whole selves to work.  I’d love to work the way YOU want to work.  So the freer you are in sharing what cadence and style works for you, the happier I am.  I believe it’s part of my job to figure out how you work best and adjust to that, especially when it comes to those I have the privilege to lead.

### Short and Frequent {#short-and-frequent}

I believe in a regular cadence of meetings and I understand that’s already the norm.  Short and frequent works well, so I suspect I’ll be inclined to adapt to many of the existing meeting norms.

### Structured but Relaxed {#structured-but-relaxed}

I tend to operate informally, but enjoy a structured approach – even if it’s as simple as 3 topics on a verbal agenda

### Visual Learner {#visual-learner}

I learn best visually, especially with images, charts…even pictures

### Metaphors and Analogies {#metaphors-and-analogies}

I’m big on metaphors and analogies – and I admit to mixing them frequently.  Feel free to roll your eyes.

### Pump the brakes, if necessary {#pump-the-brakes,-if-necessary}

I like to move quickly, so don’t be afraid to pump the brakes

### Email is the best bet {#email-is-the-best-bet}

I’ll use any communication tool, but email is my go-to.  I really like to talk to people, especially when the topic is complex.  Text is fine, too, especially after about 8 or on the weekends, when I’m less likely to be checking email.  You’ll see me on Slack, but it’s more of an occasional thing than a habit.  

## How I plan to start: {#how-i-plan-to-start:}

We will take the first 100 days seriously.  You can expect me to:

### Ask Questions {#ask-questions}

I’ll ask lots of questions.  Don’t bother trying to figure out where I’m going with them…it’ll take me a while before I’m educated enough to have a deeply held perspective other than the desire to learn.

### Meet People\! {#meet-people!}

I’ll work to meet as many people as possible. Want to meet everybody (I know I can’t, but I can’t help trying\!)

### Focus on Credit {#focus-on-credit}

We'll spend a particularly large amount of time on credit.  (I’ve been wanting a peek under that hood for quite some time.)

### Day 100 {#day-100}

I will come back to you at (or around) day 100 with a full readout of what I’ve learned, what I now believe to be true, what I still don’t know, and what – if anything – we’ll do differently

## Two Final Thoughts {#two-final-thoughts}

There are 2 things I think are especially important for any leader in a transition.  The first is to pay close attention to everything you’re thinking – but to write it all down.  Often these early observations lead to something great – but there’s almost always a story behind every “why is this the way that it is” question.

The second is that it’s important for every team to win, and to get wins.  But I don’t subscribe to the belief that every new leader needs to manufacture early wins.  We’ll figure out the long-term plan together, so that we can win the most and over the longest-term possible.  That may mean some points on the board early, and it may not.  Wherever the analytical journey takes us, we’ll do the right things, together.
